title: Labor bets house on tax reform, but may wreck the economy
full_text:
As the longest serving chief executive of any Australian bank in history, David Murray knows how to weigh up big bets on the economy.
The former Commonwealth Bank boss, who reigned during the Keating and Howard era reforms of superannuation and GST, has weighed up the Albanese government’s big tax and housing gamble and he doesn’t like the odds.
The bet, placed by Jim Chalmers with a nod of approval from Anthony Albanese, is to make the biggest changes to capital gains tax, negative gearing and trusts in a generation, all in a bid to win the political narrative of fixing so-called intergenerational inequality with improved first-home buyer numbers, more redistributed wealth and an improvement in Australia’s economic growth.
“These tax changes are driven out of ideology. It is true that house prices are too high for people in the workforce and people can’t get in, and I’m sensitive to that, but this approach to tax changes won’t fix the problem,” Murray tells Inquirer.
“The issue is all about supply, and the way you fix it is by fixing the broader economy through productivity, proper tax reform on corporate rates, GST, personal tax rates, which help temper house price growth but also help incomes catch up.” But the big bet comes at a risky time. There have been three interest rate rises, inflation is sticking above the Reserve Bank’s target, unemployment has drifted up to 4.5 per cent this week from 4.1 per cent at the start of the year, productivity rates have turned negative and been downgraded twice by the RBA and Treasury, and softer GDP figures have come through and are expected early next month.
“When I was CEO I may have said house prices were going too high, but trying to edge them down with policy changes is not effective,” Murray says. “It will lead to a downturn in housing and that has a wealth effect and that will slow the economy.” To some, the bet could go either way – it could pay off for the government. It also could leave the economy heading south which, so far, is the direction the compass arrow seems to be pointing.
Australia’s Home Value Index fell 0.7 per cent in July, the largest monthly drop since the Covid era. It dropped 0.4 per cent in June, immediately following the budget.
As home prices fall, some home buyers want to avoid catching a falling knife. In the past fortnight, all four big banks have reported falls in home loan applications across all types of buyers.
The Commonwealth Bank revealed a 28 per cent collapse in investor loan applications since, specifically, the May budget. The bank, which is the country’s biggest residential lender, also reported a 9 per cent slide in owner-occupier applications.
Westpac reported an overall 20 per cent drop in mortgage applications specifically since the May budget. It also downgraded its forecasts for home loan lending growth for investors and owner-occupiers. National Australia Bank showed investor home loan applications fell 16 per cent, with the decline accelerating post-budget. Owner-occupier borrowers fell 14 per cent. ANZ was off 12 per cent overall while Aussie Home Loans revealed a 20 per cent drop.
For the Albanese government, whose key bet is about getting more younger people into the housing market, last Friday’s official lending figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics would have been a shock.
Both first-home buyer categories – those whose first property purchase they will live in and those whose first property purchase they will lease out – showed a decline in home loan commitments, down 3 per cent and 14 per cent respectively.
This week Stockland, the biggest listed residential developer in Australia, said inquiry volumes were “down in the fourth quarter following cumulative interest rate increases and tax changes”, while Mirvac, another listed developer, noted “moderation of sales activity and inquiry” in the same period.
The second largest developer, Nigel Satterley, who sells about 3500 properties a year, says rents are about to rise 15 to 20 per cent and that first-home buyer inquiry has dropped 50 per cent since the May budget.
“The rental increases will be about 15 to 20 per cent over the next two years or about 7.5 per cent per annum,” Satterley tells Inquirer. “Investors know there’s a shortage, and what they’re saying to us now at the coalface is, ‘We’re going to build a new rental home and we won’t be selling it because of the new rules’, because if they sell it the percentage of tax has increased.
“When the market is normal the demand for lots is 50,000 per annum and our forecast for this year will be about 32,000,” he says.
Asked “what is that attributed to”, Satterley says, “The new budget and the changes to the rules. It’s made the buyers very cautious because the investors can’t buy established houses and get a tax deduction.” Lower house prices, lower auction clearance rates and lower home sales have dreadful effects on consumption, which itself makes up more than half of overall GDP. Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock said last week she was surprised by the “speed and extent” of the property market downturn.
The RBA has modelled the impacts on consumption from the so-called wealth effect of falling house prices.
“A fall in housing prices affects the economy in several ways. As well as lowering net wealth and household consumption, lower housing prices also reduce incentives to build new housing,” the RBA states in an analysis.
“The components of consumption that respond most to changes in wealth are typically durable goods, such as motor vehicles and household furnishings.” It’s no wonder furniture giant Nick Scali revealed this month that a “negative wealth effect” had led to a 10 per cent drop in store traffic.
“We rely on what we call replacement, people that refurbish and then people moving (home) and that drives furniture sales,” Nick Scali boss Anthony Scali says.
Retailers such as JB Hi-Fi copped a record share price hit after reporting its results this week, while Myer reported a slump in sales in June and July, and Macquarie noted retail brands Rebel, Boating Camping and Fishing and Macpac were “continuing to underperform v CPI and our expectations”.
The RBA set out fresh forecasts last week anticipating a lower rate of consumption for the rest of the year than it expected before the May budget.
Despite all the signs in the economy, Labor’s big bet is going double or nothing.
There are no signs of repealing the negative gearing policy in the same way Paul Keating did in 1987. He had banned the practice in 1985 and had also included grandfathering provisions.
Playing down the prospect of higher rents this week, Chalmers confirmed the key number he was betting on: first-home buyers.
“The best way to put downward pressure on rents over time is to build more homes, and also to help more renters become first-home buyers, which is, you know, really one of the fundamental objectives of our ambitious tax reform package – to make it easier for people to buy their first home,” the Treasurer said.
On budget night Chalmers declared he would have an extra “75,000 Australians achieve the dream of home ownership”.
In the year leading up to the May budget, 127,889 first-home buyers were already entering the home loan market, with about 7000 of those first-home buyers buying their home as an investment, analysis by The Australian shows.
For Chalmers to take the mantle of bringing in the most first-home buyers into the market in one year, unadjusted for the historically high immigration rates, he will need to beat Liberal treasurer Josh Frydenberg’s record in the year to September 2021 when 181,157 first-home buyers entered.
But this big bet on Labor bringing in more first-home buyers comes at the expense of pushing out investors.
The Prime Minister says pushing out investors is the price to pay after “taxpayer-funded landlord welfare” fuelled years of house price jumps that now have the median house value 8.9 times the average income.
Housing Minister Clare O’Neil also declared this week in parliament that Labor had “brought to an end” a system that enabled investors to compete at auctions. But what is the real cost of pushing out investors and pulling in what Treasury has estimated would be 75,000 extra first-home buyers and 65,000 new properties?
Modelling by Bob Scealy, director of quantitative economics consulting firm Qaive, and Tulipwood Economics director Joe Branigan show the cost to the overall economy of Labor winning this bet is likely to be up to $500,000 per new home to be built and bring each extra first-home buyer into the market. This is calculated through the standard economic rule of marginal excess burden.
“The changes in tax do not in itself create overall wealth or subtract from overall wealth – it just transfers it. But the marginal excess burden is the cost of that transfer – the administrative and compliance costs, the frictional operational costs and the behavioural changes such as lost production or consumption due to the incentives from that tax change,” Scealy says.
“When governments raise money through taxes it comes at a cost. Treasury measures some of these ‘excess burdens’ in the Henry Tax review. More up-to-date estimates have the marginal excess burden of these taxes at about 32c in the dollar of tax raised.” Treasury said in the budget the tax changes would reduce housing supply by about 35,000 homes before extra money would lift supply to 65,000. The economists say that applying the 32c to the forecast $43bn in property tax changes on a net 30,000 homes means the cost is about $500,000 per new home.
“The government’s housing package raises $43bn in extra tax and claims at most 30,000 net additional homes. Once the additional federal infrastructure expenditure and plausible state delivery costs are included, even a conservative marginal excess burden of 30c in the dollar implies about $15bn of deadweight loss – roughly half a million dollars for every net additional home,” Branigan says.
“There has been a lot of competition in the first quarter of this century for ‘worst ever public policy’, but for me this is it.” While the concerns of higher median house values – now estimated at 8.9 times the average income – are powerful in voter land, economists such as Branigan say you have to consider other factors.
“It is true that the house-price-to-income ratio has risen sharply, and that is a genuine affordability failure,” Branigan says.
“Two-income household borrowing capacity, structurally lower interest rates and bigger houses built to higher regulatory standards explain part of the long-run shift. But they do not excuse the missing low-cost housing that young people desperately need.
“Governments need to release cheaper serviced land, make faster approvals and the availability of fit-for-purpose homes that can be built fast will help. Taxing the very people who invest in housing and trying to paper over bad tax policy with even worse fiscal policy is not the answer.” While the cost is high to the economy, there also are no assurances on supply. Treasury secretary Jenny Wilkinson says the tax reforms outlined in the budget were not necessarily about increasing the aggregate supply of housing and instead designed to change the “distribution of ownership”.
“In aggregate, I think the better way to think about the impact of these tax changes is about changing the distribution of ownership rather than them being central to changing the sort of supply itself,” she told the Australian Business Economists forum on May 29.
But regardless of the cost, politicians pay top dollar to win these big bets on political narratives. Conservative-leaning pollster Australian Institute for Progress executive director Graham Young has produced polls that show Labor is indeed winning this narrative on housing.
In his most recent polling the government fared better on the two new housing-specific tax changes. The capital gains changes were approved by an overall 47 per cent of voters and disapproved by 40 per cent.
Among ALP-aligned voters, 90 per cent approved, while only 5 per cent of Coalition voters and 4 per cent of One Nation voters approved. On negative gearing changes 50 per cent approved and 38 per cent disapproved. There was a similar reflection of approval and disapproval based on party alignment.
“Supporters of the changes cluster around fairness, competition from investors for stock, housing access and a level playing field. Conservative opposition clustered around incentives, investment, rental supply, business risk and prices,” Young says.
“This makes support unusually exposed to events.
“If rents rise or housing supply contracts, opponents gain evidence for their causal argument; if affordability improves without damaging rental supply, the government’s argument is strengthened.” For Murray, the tax changes are an expensive price to pay for winning a narrative. He says if you really needed to change CGT and negative gearing “you would take the recommendation from the Ralph review which said that maybe 50 per cent discount was too generous and you could peg it back to 40 per cent”, while on negative gearing “you could look at, say, neutral gearing as an option”.
“It’s not good policy to deal with the tax structure on a piecemeal basis, which these tax changes did. If we haven’t dealt with productivity and inflation, what’s the point in having a shot at housing taxes in the middle of it all?” But for Chalmers and Albanese, winning the housing narrative isn’t everything; it’s the only thing.
